extraction.name: MMMU: A Massive Multi-discipline Multimodal Understanding and Reasoning Benchmark for Expert AGI
extraction.description: MMMU is a benchmark designed to evaluate multimodal models on massive multi-discipline tasks demanding college-level subject knowledge and deliberate reasoning. It includes 11.5K meticulously collected multimodal questions from college exams, quizzes, and textbooks, covering six core disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering. These questions span 30 subjects and 183 subfields, comprising 30 highly heterogeneous image types.
extraction.creator: Xiang Yue, Yuansheng Ni, Kai Zhang, Tianyu Zheng, Ruoqi Liu, Ge Zhang, Samuel Stevens, Dongfu Jiang, Weiming Ren, Yuxuan Sun, Cong Wei, Botao Yu, Ruibin Yuan, Renliang Sun, Ming Yin, Boyuan Zheng, Zhenzhu Yang, Yibo Liu, Wenhao Huang, Huan Sun, Yu Su, Wenhu Chen

extraction.rai:dataCollection: Data is primarily collected from free online resources, quizzes, textbooks, and other study materials. Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the 30 subjects assisted in question collection. They collected multimodal questions from major textbooks and online resources, creating new questions based on their expertise where necessary. The annotators were instructed to adhere to copyright and license regulations, avoiding data from sites prohibiting copy and redistribution. Given data contamination concerns, annotators were advised to select questions without immediately available answers, such as those with answers in separate documents or at the end of textbooks.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Manual Human Curator, Document analysis, Web Scraping
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Questions sourced from college exams, quizzes, textbooks, and online resources across 30 subjects spanning six disciplines: Art & Design, Business, Science, Health & Medicine, Humanities & Social Science, and Tech & Engineering.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Data quality control was performed in multiple stages. In the first stage, lexical overlap and source URL similarity were employed to identify potential duplicate problems. Suspected duplicates were reviewed by authors to identify and eliminate duplications. The second stage involved distributing problems among co-authors for format and typo checking, ensuring adherence to a standardized format and undertaking necessary corrections. In the third stage, authors categorized problems into four difficulty levels: very easy, easy, medium, and hard. Approximately 10% of problems classified as very easy and not aligning with design criteria were excluded from the benchmark.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Questions were manually collected and annotated by over 50 university students specializing in the relevant subjects. Annotators categorized each question as either multiple-choice or open-ended, annotated all fields including question text, answer options for multiple-choice questions, correct answer, image types, question difficulty, and explanation (if available). All questions were required to contain one or more images, be written in English, meet college-level difficulty, and be unambiguous. A secondary review team rigorously vetted annotations for quality and guideline adherence. Regular audits of random samples were conducted to ensure sustained quality and consistency.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: A user-friendly web interface was developed for data annotation and verification.
extraction.rai:dataReleaseMaintenancePlan: The paper mentions version changes (V1 to V4) with updates to model results, corrections, and additions. However, specific versioning information regarding updating timeframe, maintainers, and deprecation policies for the dataset itself is not explicitly stated.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The benchmark is designed to push the boundaries of what large multimodal models can achieve and is intended to be instrumental in developing next-generation multimodal foundation models and monitoring progress towards Expert AGI. The authors believe strong performance on MMMU should be a necessary criterion for an Expert AGI system to demonstrate broad and deep subject knowledge as well as expert-level understanding and reasoning capabilities.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The manual curation process may carry biases. The focus on college-level subjects might not be sufficient for testing Expert AGI. The benchmark combines multiple-choice questions with concise open-ended questions to balance complexity and practicality, but this may not capture all aspects of expert-level reasoning. The paper notes that MMMU is not a sufficient test for Expert AGI as there lacks a direct mapping between performance on MMMU and '90th percentile of skilled adults,' nor are college exams the only tasks an AGI shall tackle.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is designed for evaluating multimodal models on college-level multi-discipline tasks. Use cases include Testing and Validation of large multimodal models (LMMs) to assess their capabilities in expert-level perception, knowledge recall, and reasoning across diverse disciplines. The benchmark is intended to monitor progress towards Expert AGI and stimulate the community to build next-generation multimodal foundation models.
extraction.rai:annotationsPerItem: For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students (3 per subject) completed 30 questions each in their corresponding subjects, totaling 900 validation questions. For the main dataset, each question has one correct answer annotated.
extraction.rai:annotatorDemographics: Over 50 university students, including co-authors, specializing in the 30 subjects covered by the benchmark. For human expert evaluation, 90 college senior students were selected to represent experts in the corresponding 30 subjects (3 student experts per subject).
